gaps.list: §25(e)(1)(C) applicable tax limit for the mortgage credit certificate credit: §26(a) limit reduced by subpart credits 'other than this section and sections 23 and 25D'
gaps.effect: §25F(f)(1) uses the same formula without carving out §25, and §25(e)(1)(C) was not amended to carve out §25F. Each credit's limit is reduced by the other, so when the two exceed the tax left both are cut back and total credits allowed fall below the tax. With §25F read into the §25 list (or §25 into §25F's) the credits absorb the whole tax and one excess carries forward.
gaps.example: 2027: tax after other credits $2,500, mortgage credit $2,000, scholarship gift $1,700. Literal: §25 limit 2,500-1,700=$800, §25F limit 2,500-2,000=$500; $1,300 allowed, $1,200 tax paid, $1,200 of each credit carried forward (3 and 5 years). Ordered reading: $2,500 allowed, tax $0, $1,200 carried. Best alternative: give only $500 and lose nothing, so it bites the taxpayer who gives the full $1,700.
gaps.could_cover: §25F(h) guidance power; IRS form worksheets normally fix credit order; reading 'allowable' as post-limit gives simultaneous equations, not a fix. Timing only if later years have room; permanent if facts repeat and carryforwards expire.
gaps.confidence: high that the text is circular; medium that it costs money in practice

gaps.new: §72(t)(2)(H) birth/adoption $5,000, (I) emergency $1,000, (K) domestic abuse $10,000, (M) disaster $22,000, (N) long-term care
gaps.list: §72(t)(2)(B), (E), (F): withdrawals already exempt under (A), (C), (D) [and (B), (E)] are not counted against the medical, tuition and $10,000 first-home allowances
gaps.effect: The newer exempt withdrawals are not in those lists, so on the words they count against the capped allowances; an IRA owner with both kinds in one year can be left with 10% additional tax on the overlap. Read in, no additional tax.
gaps.example: $5,000 birth withdrawal plus $10,000 more from an IRA with $10,000 tuition: $0 if (H) is in the (E) list; 10% x $5,000 = $500 on the government's reading. Disaster version ($22,000 + $22,000 tuition): $2,200.
gaps.could_cover: 'to the extent' in (E) and 'may be treated as' in §72(t)(8)(B) let the taxpayer assign the capped exception to the other dollars; return-form practice is not known to stack (unchecked); first-home overlap avoidable by not tracing the money to the purchase.
